title: Remembering
hookLine: a memorial prayer on Yom Kippur and the last days of festivals
tomorrow: Who by fire, who by water

cards: It's the last day of a festival. The synagogue is fuller than usual. Then the rabbi announces Yizkor, and something unusual happens.
A handful of people, often younger ones, stand up and walk out. Not rudely. Quietly, as if on cue.
They'll wait in the hallway and come back in a few minutes. The people who stay have someone to remember. Inside, the room gets very still.
People hold small prayer books close to their faces. Some are crying. Some just stare at a name.

teach.b: Yizkor means may he remember. The prayer begins: may God remember the soul of my father, or my mother, or my husband, my wife, my child, my friend, and the listener fills in the name.

In Ashkenazi communities it's said four times a year: on Yom Kippur, and on the last day of Passover, of Shavuot, and of Sukkot, at Shemini Atzeret. Each time, in the middle of a festival, the community stops to remember.
Where did it come from? Some historians trace it to the Rhineland, in the time of the Crusades, when whole Jewish communities were killed.
Survivors kept memorial books with the names of the dead, and read them aloud. What began as remembering martyrs became remembering everyone.
Many Sephardi communities have their own memorial prayers, called hashkavah, said at other times.
Part of Yizkor, for many, is a promise to give charity in the person's memory. The idea is that the living can do good on someone's behalf, so that their life keeps doing good.
And then there's the custom you saw in the hook. In many communities, people whose parents are living leave the room during Yizkor. Some say it's to avoid tempting fate by standing among mourners.
Others say it's out of kindness, to give the bereaved privacy.
It's a folk custom, not a law, and plenty of people stay to remember others. And some prayer books add a prayer for the Jews killed in the Holocaust, for whom no one else may be left to say a name.

how: Yizkor is said in Ashkenazi synagogues on Yom Kippur, Shemini Atzeret, the last day of Passover and the second day of Shavuot (outside Israel); each person inserts the names of those they remember and often pledges charity, and many with living parents step out.

games.q: both your parents are alive. the rabbi announces Yizkor. what do many people in your place do?
o: leave the room for a few minutes.
games.why: in many communities they step out, a folk custom; others stay to remember grandparents, friends or Holocaust victims.

practice: Bring to mind someone who has died, a parent, a grandparent, a friend, a teacher, even someone you never met but carry, and say their name out loud, once.
Then picture one ordinary thing about them, their hands, their laugh, the way they said your name, and stay with it.

carryVoice: Your line: remember them. Their names are still worth saying, out loud. See you tomorrow.
